Chart system 01 · A concept for Board 3

Explainer

Explainer leads with the finding. Each chart opens with the kind of evidence and a sentence that says what the data shows, and notes in the drawing teach what a reader could otherwise miss.

Charts sit in one reading column, the way an explainer runs, and four break wider where the data needs room. The scenario chart is a table, because a reader looks it up. No chart on these views takes the working red; the system sheet shows how red behaves.

ShowHide how to read our charts, in short
  1. The black label names the kind of evidence. A Finding is something measured; an Estimate depends on stated assumptions.
  2. The title is the answer in one sentence. “Would” or “may” in a title marks a less certain claim.
  3. The gray line under the title says what was counted, in what unit, where and when.
  4. The dark mark is what the title is about; gray marks are there to compare.
  5. Notes in and under the chart explain anything drawn in an unusual way, such as a line that breaks.
  6. The source line says who collected the numbers. Open the table under any chart to see every value.

S01 Big number in context

Reader question
Do Republicans and Democrats agree on anything about Congress?
Why this form
One large figure gives the fact a reader repeats; the party bars and the two votes put it in context in the same drawing.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S02 Line with event notes

Reader question
What happened to child poverty when the expanded child tax credit was paid, and after it lapsed?
Why this form
A line shows the rise and fall in order, and notes at 2021, 2025 and the method breaks explain what a reader could misread.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S03 Ranked bar

Reader question
Who changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?
Why this form
Ranked bars answer who acted most, and splitting each bar by the atlas’s direction code shows which way each instrument moved the rules.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S04 Dot plot or dumbbell

Reader question
Which age groups vote, and did that change between two elections?
Why this form
A dumbbell puts two elections on one line for each age group, so the level and the change read at once.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S05 Small multiples

Reader question
How far apart are homeownership rates by race, and has the gap closed?
Why this form
Small multiples give each group its own panel on one scale, so a reader follows one line at a time and still sees the others.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S06 Comparison table

Reader question
If a reform path were followed, which way would each outcome move?
Why this form
A table lets a reader look up one scenario and one outcome; the atlas’s own words sit in every cell beside our arrow.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S07 Map

Reader question
Where can a city adopt ranked-choice voting, and where has the state ruled it out?
Why this form
A tile map gives each state the same weight, so the count reads true where a land map would favor large western states.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S08 Unit chart

Reader question
Have the rules been moving toward voters or away from them?
Why this form
One square per entry lets a reader count, and placing toward above the year band and away below it shows both sides of the log at once.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S09 Timeline

Reader question
Which rule changes since 1870 decided who counts, who governs, who owns and who checks?
Why this form
A true time scale shows when the atlas’s picks bunch together, and four lanes keep each thread readable.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S10 Evidence mix

Reader question
How much of each everyday answer rests on documented fact?
Why this form
A bar split by grade shows how much of each answer rests on the record, and sorting by that share puts the answers in order.

Chart system 01 · Explainer

On Charcoal

Two charts with the proposed dark palette. Newsprint carries the subject; Dim Newsprint carries secondary text; context lines take Stone mixed 35 percent toward Newsprint; gridlines drop to Stone mixed 45 percent toward Charcoal. On Charcoal, lifted Prussian and lifted Verdigris land too close to tell apart, so dark charts keep to few categories and label every series directly. The grade ramp steps from Newsprint to Stone mixed 35 percent toward Newsprint, then Stone, then a hatch, so it keeps its order by lightness.

Chart system 01 · Explainer

Social card

One chart as a portrait post at 1080 by 1350 pixels, the size Instagram and LinkedIn use. It is chart S01 from the same generator, with type at one and a quarter times its page size so labels hold at a phone’s feed width. The card keeps the evidence label, the title, the measure line, the full source and the wordmark, so it still makes sense when it travels without the page. It names Oath & Action and the atlas and carries no web address until the site is settled. It sits on Newsprint, the ground a feed of white cards does not use.

How to read our charts

For readers, in plain words. This guide can run under any chart or on a help page; every chart links here.

  1. Start with the label. The black chip says what kind of evidence the chart shows. A Finding is something measured, with a source and a period. An Association links two things without showing that one caused the other. An Estimate says what would happen if stated assumptions hold. An Illustration shows how a chart works, with made-up numbers, and says so beside the chart.
  2. Read the title as the answer. It is one sentence that says what the numbers show, and its verb tells you how sure it is. Record words such as “passed” and “fell” mean the facts are on the public record. “Raises” or “lowers” means strong research evidence. “Can” or “may” means some evidence. “Would” means an estimate that depends on assumptions. “Untested” means nobody has tested it yet. When the evidence is disputed, the title gives both readings.
  3. Check what was counted. The gray line under the title names what was measured, in what unit, where and when, and says when the scale does not start at zero.
  4. Look for the dark mark. The dark line, bar or dot is what the title is about. Gray marks are there for comparison. A chart that shows evidence grades uses shade for the grade instead, and says so.
  5. Read the notes in and under the chart. Short notes point at the record, the turning point or anything drawn in an unusual way, such as a line that breaks where a survey changed.
  6. Allow for survey error. Survey numbers come from a sample of people, so each has a margin of error. A margin of 0.5 points means the true figure most likely sits within half a point either way, and a smaller change may be chance.
  7. Red marks one thing. When a chart uses red, it marks the single point the title names, or the step you can take now. Red never stands for a party, a side, or good or bad.
  8. Find where the numbers came from. The source line names who collected the data, when, and what to keep in mind. Open the table under any chart to see every value and every note.

Chart S02 with every part numbered.

2Child poverty fell to 5.1 percent in 2021, the lowest since the series began in 2009, and more than doubled the next year.

3Children under 18 below the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts tax credits and other aid, percent, United States, 2009 to 2025; the official measure, which counts pretax cash income only, in gray.

Figures for 2019 to 2024 include the Bureau’s August 2026 revision and differ by up to 0.4 points from those first published.

How to read our charts · Chart: Oath & Action

14+ Show the table and notes

  1. Evidence label. The kind of evidence in a dark chip: Finding, Association, Estimate or Illustration. The grade follows in words.
  2. Title. One sentence that states the finding, in Inter Tight 800. Its verb matches the grade: record words for documented, “can” or “may” for plausible, “would” for a scenario.
  3. Measure line. The measure, unit, place and period, in Inter 400 Deep Stone. It says when a scale is cropped and what each measure counts.
  4. Unit on the top tick. The unit appears once, on the top tick or the first label. Other ticks stay bare.
  5. Gridlines. Horizontal 1 px hairlines in the grid tint. No vertical grid and no tick marks. A gridline passes behind a label, never through it.
  6. Baseline. A 1.5 px Charcoal line at zero. Bars always start here.
  7. Subject. The series the title names: 3 px Charcoal, labeled directly in Inter 600.
  8. Context. Other series in 2 px Stone, labeled in Deep Stone. They recede so the subject reads first.
  9. Point label. The value the title names, printed beside its point in Inter 600.
  10. Note and leader. Notes sit in open space in Inter 14 px Deep Stone, 45 to 75 characters a line, joined to the data by a 1 px leader at least 12 px long, with one bend at most.
  11. Odd encoding, explained once. Here the steps at 2013, 2017 and 2019 are method breaks. The line never bridges them.
  12. End note. A note in open space names the value a reader would look for, and the event that bears on it.
  13. Source line, guide link and credit. Publisher, table, period, geography, date retrieved and the qualification, in that order. “How to read our charts” and the credit sit at right.
  14. Table and notes. One click opens every value and every note; the toggle names the chart and shows whether it is open.

Evidence grades

One table sets each grade’s words, mark and title verbs for every chart that draws grades. Grades never take red, and a chart that shades by grade says so in its key.

One grade table for every chart
GradeMeansTitle verbs
Documentedon the public recordrecord language: passed, ruled, was
Well supportedstrong research evidencea direct finding: raises, lowers
Plausiblesome evidence“can” or “may”
Contestedevidence disputedboth readings, side by side
Hypothesisnot yet tested“untested”

Type

The locked faces only. Inter Tight sets titles and big numbers, Inter sets every label and number, and Lora Italic appears only for quoted words. Figures take tabular widths; words never do, so a hyphen keeps its width. Nothing on screen goes under 13 px.

Marks

Line weights follow the studio’s family of 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 6 px (D2-60). Each drawing comes at 1,024 or 720, 600, 358 and 328 px and shows at its natural size, so no weight scales up.

Color, measured on each ground

Every chart color is a role, and every tint is an OKLab mix of locked colors with one job. Contrast is measured against the ground (WCAG 2.x). Text needs 4.5:1; a mark needs 3:1; a fill under 3:1 is used only where every value is printed or the table carries it, which is a design judgment. Categories never rest on Verdigris against Stone alone: they sit 0.05 apart in OKLab lightness, so position, fill or a label carries them too. In forced colors, tints drop away and the glyph or label carries the meaning.

Notes and source lines

Notes

  • Name the record, give a reader’s scale, or explain an unusual encoding once. A note that does none of these comes out.
  • Put a short note in open space near its data and join it with a 1 px Stone leader, at least 12 px long, with one bend at most. Leaders and rules never cross a label; a gridline passes behind one.
  • Keep notes in the drawing short. Longer notes, the coding rules and any disclosure sit in HTML under the drawing, 45 to 75 characters a line, where they wrap.
  • State the qualification where it changes the reading: self-reported rates, method breaks, a survey older than the votes, the one entry that stands for many.
  • A note may say what a measure did over time. It never says a policy caused it unless the source grades that cause.
  • Label series at the line or the bar. Use a key only when labels cannot fit, and draw the key in the chart’s own marks.
  • Read every title twice before it ships, once as a reader on the left and once as a reader on the right. If either would take it as a side, rewrite it.

Source lines

  • Order: publisher, title or table, observation period, geography, date retrieved, qualification (Master Brief section 15).
  • Start from the dataset’s source line. Shorten only by dropping words, never facts. Dates read as words and never break across a line.
  • Inter 400, 13/18, Deep Stone, under a grid-tint hairline, with “How to read our charts” and “Chart: Oath & Action” at the right.
  • A compiled list says so in the line, as the ranked-choice map does for Ballotpedia.
  • Charts on nomination, ranked-ballot or election-rule data print the editor’s disclosure word for word, labeled “Disclosure:”, with the chart.
  • The table under every chart repeats the source, so the equivalent stands on its own.

Red, once

Rule 05.3, as Dustin approved it (D2-01):

“The wordmark’s ampersand and the lockmark’s lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon’s red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline’s ampersand uses the view’s working red. The hinge divider’s ampersand takes its surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian.”

On a chart page each chart counts as one view. A chart posted alone may mark the point its title names in red; a chart added to a page takes red only when the page’s red job moves to it. The ten charts in this concept take no working red: the one candidate, the 2021 low in S02, sits on a year most readers tie to one policy, so the demonstrations use the Senate shortfall in S01. Party marks, grades, scales and categories never take red.

Demonstration A, a specimen

Title for this demonstration: The Senate vote to take up the ban fell 7 votes short of the 60 needed.

With nothing else in the view asking for red, the shortfall the title names takes it. Red marks the one point the title names.

Demonstration B, a specimen: an ask takes the red

Same title. The view now holds a step the reader can take.

See how your senators voted Illustrative ask

The step a reader can take now outranks the point the title names, so the ask keeps the red and the shortfall steps down to the darkest ink.

The chart kit

The generators in build_concept.py, the seed of the kit (DR-49). Each takes a width and data from the shared dataset and returns a drawing that has passed the label guard. No chart here moves; an animated chart must offer a still version for readers who ask for reduced motion.

Generators
CallWhat it draws
gen_s01(W, uid, t=None, compact=False, red=None)Big number, party bars and two votes. compact drops notes for a card; red marks the Senate shortfall for the red demonstration.
gen_s02(W, uid, t=None, anatomy=False)Line with event notes and method breaks, from rows with year, percent and comparable_with.
gen_s03(W, uid, t=None)Ranked bar split by a category code; short labels at the bars are chosen from the data.
gen_s04(W, uid, t=None)Dumbbell for two years per group; the scale and the words for a small change come from the data.
gen_s05(W, uid, t=None)Small multiples on one scale, one panel per group, breaks where the method changed.
gen_s06_table(view)Comparison table with the source words in every cell and a boxed glyph for the reading.
gen_s07(W, uid, t=None)Tile map from the shared tile grid, one square per state.
gen_s08(W, uid, t=None)Unit chart: one square per record, by year column, with per-year counts and a roll-up mark.
gen_s09(W, uid, t=None)Timeline on a true time scale with lanes; labels stack so no leader crosses a label.
gen_s10(W, uid, t=None)One 100 percent bar per row from the grade table, with the count beside each share.
figure(view, spec) and specimen(view, sid)The frame, built from one spec object: evidence label, title, measure, drawing, notes, disclosure, source with the guide link, and the table toggle. A new chart passes its dataset, evidence kind, grade line and source in the spec; S01 to S10 look theirs up by ID.
copy(s), source_text(dataset) and nw(n)The copy pipeline: curly quotes and apostrophes, dates in words with no break inside, the true minus, record codes kept off source lines, and numbers in words to 99 (it stops the build beyond that).
Art(W, uid) with text(), para(), line(), path(), leader() and render()The drawing: render() refuses a label that collides, leaves the drawing or is crossed by a line.
